connector: By Chapter 13, Harriet was leading people all the way to Canada, and still going back for more. In Chapter 14 the enslaved people begin calling her by a new name. As you read, list every reason that name fits, and decide which one matters most.

a.raw: everyone said she led them faithfully the song called her moses gently
a.fixed: Everyone said she led them faithfully. The song called her Moses gently.
a.why: Capital E starts the sentence; a period ends the first sentence; capital T starts the second; capital M on Moses (a name). Faithfully and gently are adverbs that tell how.

b.raw: harriet planned each trip carefully she never acted recklessly
b.fixed: Harriet planned each trip carefully. She never acted recklessly.
b.why: Capital H on Harriet; a period ends the first sentence; capital S starts the second. Carefully and recklessly tell how; never tells how often.

fill1.h1: Pushing back a laugh in a quiet room. Which root means push?
fill1.why: press means push: re + press = push back, hold in.

fill2.h1: Saying what you think pushes it out into words. Which root means push?
fill2.why: press means push: ex + press = push out.

fill3.h1: Food holds you up through a long day. Which root means hold?
fill3.why: tain means hold: sus + tain = hold up, keep going.

fill4.h1: To get something, you take hold of it. Which root means hold?
fill4.why: tain means hold: ob + tain = take hold of.

notes.wgrd: When many causes lead to one result, list them all. Take each one away and ask if the result still happens. The one it can’t do without matters most.
vocab: The act of ending something, especially slavery.
A guide on the Underground Railroad; or, the person who runs a train.
To make a thought, feeling, or idea known to others.
notes.wordParts: press means “push” and tain means “hold”: express, impress, contain, obtain.
notes.grammar: Cut adverbs that do no work. If a sentence says the same thing without the extra word, leave it out, or choose a stronger verb.
notes.spelling: The suffixes -ive, -al, and -ic turn a word into a describing word: act → active, music → musical, hero → heroic. Look at the base word first. Sometimes a letter drops, like a silent e.

wordgame.voice: Tap a root, then the word it finishes. Or drag the root onto the word. Ask what each word is about: pushing, or holding?

why.t: In Chapter 2, Harriet’s mother, Old Rit, finishes a patchwork quilt, the family’s only treasure. Years later, in Chapter 12, Harriet tucks that same quilt over her parents’ legs as she drives them out of slavery. press means push, and tain means hold. Each right word sews one patch into the quilt. Four each lesson, until the quilt is finished.

wordgame.winDay: Four more patches are sewn in. The next lesson’s words add more.
wordgame.win: Old Rit’s quilt is finished, and a North Star is stitched across its middle. press = push, tain = hold.

transcripts.welcome: Hey, it’s Marcus. Harriet has gone back into Maryland again and again, and people start calling her by a new name. Chapter 14 is called Moses. On my walking tours, this was the chapter kids asked about most. Today’s question: why that name, and what does it say about how people see her?
transcripts.read: As you read, list every reason people might call Harriet Moses. There are more than you’d think. Watch her disguises and her signals, and the posters that describe her. Then rank your reasons. Which one would the name fall apart without?
transcripts.grammar: Last day with adverbs, and today you’re the editor. Some little words sound like they add a lot, but say nothing at all. Read each sentence without the extra word. If nothing is lost, cut it. If the verb feels weak, find a stronger one.

virtue.title: The freedom meter
virtue.intro: Think about one part of Chapter 14.
virtue.moment: Slaveowners put up posters and offer bigger and bigger rewards, until Harriet is worth $40,000 to anyone who catches her. She keeps going back until she has led more than three hundred people out.
virtue.ask: How much did the rewards change what Harriet did? Slide to show.
virtue.placeholder: The rewards changed Harriet this much because…
virtue.take: One way to see it: not at all. Sterling writes, “Fearless, she was never reckless.”
virtue.name: freedom
